evidence_found: Definition supporting the reading: "Reported data include all monthly net billings (shipments) between semiconductor manufacturers and their end customers, authorized distributors and divisions or subsidiaries that manufacture end products." original_interpretation: Distributor resale is not counted a second time in the WSTS market: a chip sold through a distributor enters once, at the manufacturer's billing price to the distributor, so the WSTS total excludes distributor margins.

evidence_found: "All billings are reported according to customer shipment location." evidence_found: "...imposes a license requirement for all items subject to the EAR and a license review policy of presumption of denial. Similarly, no license exceptions are available for exports, reexports, or transfers (in-country) to the persons being added to the Entity List in this rule except as allowed in the Savings Clause" (84 FR 22961, Background)
original_interpretation: For the Huawei entries added in May 2019, BIS imposed a licence requirement for all items subject to the EAR with a licence review policy of presumption of denial.

evidence_found: API record 2020-10856: citation "85 FR 29849", publication_date 2020-05-19, effective_on 2020-05-15; abstract: "This rule amends General Prohibition Three, also known as the foreign-produced direct product rule ... to impose a new control over certain foreign-produced items, when there is knowledge that such items are destined to a designated entity on the Entity List. A foreign-produced item is subject to the new control if the entity for which the item is destined has a footnote 1 designation in the Entity List. This rule also applies this new control to Huawei Technologies Co., Ltd. (Huawei) and its non-U.S. affiliates listed as entities."
original_interpretation: On 19 May 2020 (effective 15 May 2020) BIS published an interim final rule at 85 FR 29849 amending General Prohibition Three, the foreign-produced direct product rule, to control certain foreign-produced items destined to Entity List entities with a 'footnote 1' designation, and applied it to Huawei and its listed affiliates.

correction: The plant limb was conjunctive, not an alternative: an item made in a non-US plant built with US-origin technology/software was caught only if it was also the direct product of software/technology produced or developed by Huawei (e.g. a Huawei design). The first limb covered Huawei-produced technology/software (e.g. IC designs) that was itself the direct product of US-controlled technology/software in specified Cat 3/4/5 ECCNs. See superseding claim.
evidence_found: "imposes a control on the direct product of ``technology'' or ``software'' subject to the EAR, and specified in ... (ECCN) 3E001, 3E002, 3E003, 4E001, 5E001, 3D001, 4D001, or 5D001 ... produced or developed by an entity with a footnote 1 designation" and "Footnote 1 of the Entity List also applies a control to any foreign-produced item (1) that is the direct product of a plant or major component of a plant located outside the United States when the plant or major component of a plant itself is a direct product of U.S.-origin ``technology'' or ``software'' specified in ...; and (2) such item is a direct product of ``software'' or ``technology'' produced or developed by an entity with a footnote 1 designation on the Entity List." (85 FR 29849, Background)
original_interpretation: The May 2020 Huawei FDP rule reached foreign-made items that were the direct product of technology or software produced or developed by Huawei, or produced by a non-US plant that is itself a direct product of US-origin technology or software.

correction: Dates correct, but the exemption applied only to items identified in paragraph (b) of footnote 1 (the plant-based limb), not to all foreign-produced items covered by the rule.
evidence_found: "Shipments of foreign-produced items identified in paragraph (b) to footnote 1 in Supplement No. 4 of Part 744 of the EAR that are subject to Sec. 736.2(b)(3)(vi) and started ``production'' prior to May 15, 2020, are not subject to Sec. 736.2(b)(3)(vi) of the EAR ... so long as they have been exported, reexported or transferred (in-country) before September 14, 2020." (85 FR 29849, Savings clause)
original_interpretation: Under the May 2020 Huawei FDP rule, foreign-produced items that had started production before 15 May 2020 were exempt if exported, reexported or transferred before 14 September 2020.

evidence_found: API record 2020-18213: citation "85 FR 51596", publication_date 2020-08-20, effective_on 2020-08-17; abstract: "First, BIS is adding additional non-U.S. affiliates of Huawei to the Entity List ... Second, this rule removes a temporary general license for Huawei and its non-U.S. affiliates and replaces those provisions with a more limited authorization ... Third, in response to public comments, this final rule amends General Prohibition Three, also known as the foreign-produced direct product rule"
original_interpretation: The August 2020 Huawei rule is 85 FR 51596, published 20 August 2020 and effective 17 August 2020; it added more Huawei affiliates, removed Huawei's Temporary General License and amended the foreign-produced direct product rule.

correction: 38 additions is correct, but the rule attributes the 21 destinations to 'the additions and modifications' together, not to the 38 new entries alone.
evidence_found: "This rule implements the decision of the ERC to add thirty-eight additional entities to the Entity List ... The additions and modifications impact affiliates of Huawei in twenty-one different destinations: The People's Republic of China (China), Argentina, Brazil, Chile, Egypt, France, Germany, India, Israel, Mexico, Morocco, the Netherlands, Peru, Russia, Singapore, South Africa, Switzerland, Thailand, Turkey, the United Arab Emirates, and the United Kingdom." (85 FR 51596, Background A)
original_interpretation: The August 2020 rule added 38 further Huawei entities in 21 destinations to the Entity List.

correction: Substance correct, but (i) the control requires 'knowledge', it does not apply 'whenever'; (ii) the first trigger is any part, component or equipment produced, purchased or ordered by a footnote-1 entity, which is broader than 'a Huawei-produced item'; (iii) the transaction-party list is illustrative ('e.g.'), not exhaustive.
evidence_found: "You may not reexport, export from abroad, or transfer (in-country) without a license or license exception any foreign-produced item specified in paragraph (a) or (b) of this footnote when there is ``knowledge'' that: (1) The foreign-produced item will be incorporated into, or will be used in the ``production'' or ``development'' of any ``part,'' ``component,'' or ``equipment'' produced, purchased, or ordered by any entity with a footnote 1 designation ...; or (2) Any entity with a footnote 1 designation ... is a party to any transaction involving the foreign-produced item, e.g., as a ``purchaser,'' ``intermediate consignee,'' ``ultimate consignee,'' or ``end-user.''" (85 FR 51596, Supp. No. 4 to Part 744, footnote 1)
original_interpretation: The August 2020 revision made the Huawei FDP rule apply whenever a covered foreign-produced item will be incorporated into or used in the production or development of a Huawei-produced item, or when a listed Huawei entity is a purchaser, intermediate consignee, ultimate consignee or end-user, broadening the May 2020 version.

correction: Categories 3/4/5 confirmed (the 16 listed ECCNs). Limb (a) covers technology/software 'subject to the EAR', which can include foreign-origin items subject to the EAR, not only 'US technology or software'; only limb (b) requires U.S.-origin. Note also a wafer, finished or unfinished, counts as a foreign-produced item.
evidence_found: "(a) ... The foreign-produced item is a direct product of ``technology'' or ``software'' subject to the EAR and specified in Export Control Classification Number (ECCN) 3D001, 3D991, 3E001, 3E002, 3E003, 3E991, 4D001, 4D993, 4D994, 4E001, 4E992, 4E993, 5D001, 5D991, 5E001, or 5E991 ... (b) ... produced by any plant or major component of a plant that is located outside the United States, when the plant or major component of a plant, whether made in the U.S. or a foreign country, itself is a direct product of U.S.-origin ``technology'' or ``software'' subject to the EAR that is specified in [the same ECCNs]" (85 FR 51596, footnote 1(a)-(b))
original_interpretation: The August 2020 Huawei FDP rule covers foreign items that are the direct product of US technology or software, or of plants that are themselves direct products of US technology or software, specified in Categories 3, 4 and 5 of the Commerce Control List.

correction: Note: 77 entities under 78 entries; the rule also removed four entities (Israel, UAE).
evidence_found: API record 2020-28031: citation "85 FR 83416", publication 2020-12-22, effective_on 2020-12-18; abstract: "BIS amends the EAR by adding seventy-seven entities, under a total of seventy-eight entries, to the Entity List"; full text: "Semiconductor Manufacturing International Corporation Incorporated (SMIC) is added to the Entity List" (85 FR 83416, Background)
original_interpretation: BIS added 77 entities to the Entity List in a rule published at 85 FR 83416 on 22 December 2020 (effective 18 December 2020), which included SMIC.

evidence_found: "For eleven of the seventy-seven entities--SMIC and ten related entities--BIS imposes a license review policy of Presumption of Denial for items uniquely required for production of semiconductors at advanced technology nodes (10 nanometers and below, including extreme ultraviolet technology) and case by case for all other items." (85 FR 83416, Background)
original_interpretation: For SMIC, BIS set a presumption of denial for items uniquely required to produce semiconductors at 10 nm and below (including EUV technology) and case-by-case review for all other items.

evidence_found: "Semiconductor Manufacturing International Corporation Incorporated (SMIC) is added to the Entity List as a result of China's military-civil fusion (MCF) doctrine and evidence of activities between SMIC and entities of concern in the Chinese military industrial complex." (85 FR 83416, Background)
original_interpretation: BIS said SMIC was added to the Entity List as a result of China's military-civil fusion doctrine and evidence of activities between SMIC and entities of concern in the Chinese military-industrial complex.

correction: The count of 11 is stated by the rule itself, not only derived by the researcher.
evidence_found: "This rule adds SMIC and the following ten entities related to SMIC: Semiconductor Manufacturing International (Beijing) Corporation; Semiconductor Manufacturing International (Tianjin) Corporation; Semiconductor Manufacturing International (Shenzhen) Corporation; SMIC Semiconductor Manufacturing (Shanghai) Co., Ltd.; SMIC Holdings Limited; Semiconductor Manufacturing South China Corporation; SMIC Northern Integrated Circuit Manufacturing (Beijing) Co., Ltd.; SMIC Hong Kong International Company Limited; SJ Semiconductor; and Ningbo Semiconductor International Corporation (NSI)." and "eleven of the seventy-seven entities--SMIC and ten related entities" (85 FR 83416, Background)

correction: The comparison with '87 FR 47090 in the research plan' is internal bookkeeping and was not checked against any source; the citation, dates and GAAFET ECAD content are verified.

evidence_found: "These technologies are two substrates of ultra-wide bandgap semiconductors (Gallium Oxide (Ga2O3) and diamond), Electronic Computer Aided Design (ECAD) software specially designed for the development of integrated circuits with any Gate-All-Around Field-Effect Transistor (GAAFET) structure, and pressure gain combustion (PGC) technology for the production and development of gas turbine engine components or systems." and "controls decided by governments participating in the Wassenaar Arrangement ... at the December 2021 WA Plenary meeting. These four technologies meet the criteria of Section 1758" (87 FR 49979, abstract)
original_interpretation: The August 2022 rule (87 FR 49979) implemented December 2021 Wassenaar decisions on four Section 1758 technologies: gallium oxide and diamond ultra-wide bandgap substrates, ECAD software specially designed for GAAFET integrated circuits, and pressure gain combustion technology.

evidence_found: "Effective dates: This rule is effective August 15, 2022, except for instruction 5, concerning the addition of Export Control Classification Number (ECCN) 3D006, which is effective October 14, 2022." (87 FR 49979, DATES)
original_interpretation: The GAAFET ECAD software control in 87 FR 49979 (new ECCN 3D006) took effect on 14 October 2022, while the rest of the rule took effect on 15 August 2022.

correction: The 600 Gbyte/s and 4800 thresholds are right, but the October 2022 metric was 'bit length per operation x TOPS' (4800 or more), with both conditions required (600 Gbyte/s AND 4800). 'Total processing performance' was introduced only by the October 2023 AC/S IFR. See superseding claim.
evidence_found: "a. Integrated circuits that have or are programmable to have an aggregate bidirectional transfer rate over all inputs and outputs of 600 Gbyte/s or more to or from integrated circuits other than volatile memories, and any of the following: a.1. One or more digital processor units executing machine instructions having a bit length per operation multiplied by processing performance measured in TOPS, aggregated over all processor units, of 4800 or more" (87 FR 62186, instruction 26, ECCN 3A090.a); the term 'total processing performance' does not appear in 87 FR 62186. 88 FR 73458: "This AC/S IFR replaces bits x TOPS with `Total processing performance'"
original_interpretation: The October 2022 rule created ECCN 3A090 for advanced computing ICs, defined by an aggregate bidirectional transfer rate of 600 Gbyte/s and a 'total processing performance' (TPP) of 4800 or more.

correction: Historical description of the October 2022 text; later rules amended Sec. 744.23.
evidence_found: "(iii) The ``development'' or ``production'' of integrated circuits at a semiconductor fabrication ``facility'' located in the PRC that fabricates integrated circuits meeting any of the following criteria: (A) Logic integrated circuits using a non-planar transistor architecture or with a ``production'' technology node of 16/14 nanometers or less; (B) NOT AND (NAND) memory integrated circuits with 128 layers or more; or (C) Dynamic random-access memory (DRAM) integrated circuits using a ``production'' technology node of 18 nanometer half-pitch or less" (87 FR 62186, Sec. 744.23(a)(2)(iii))
original_interpretation: The October 2022 semiconductor-fabrication end-use control (15 CFR 744.23) applies to facilities in China producing logic ICs with non-planar transistors or at 16/14 nm or below, DRAM at 18 nm half-pitch or less, or NAND with 128 layers or more.

original_interpretation: The October 2023 SME rule controlled additional types of semiconductor manufacturing equipment and extended SME licence requirements beyond China and Macau to 21 other countries subject to US arms embargoes.

evidence_found: BIS page: "the AC/S IFR removes \"interconnect bandwidth\" as a parameter for identifying restricted chips. original_interpretation: The October 2023 AC/S rule removed interconnect bandwidth as a control parameter for advanced chips and replaced it with thresholds on total processing performance and a new 'performance density' parameter.

correction: Now confirmed from the full current regulatory text (both limbs). Caveat: Note 2 to 3A090.a/.b says they do not apply to items not designed or marketed for datacenters with TPP below 4800.
evidence_found: Current eCFR (Title 15 as amended to 2026-09-24), Supp. No. 1 to Part 774, ECCN 3A090: "a. Integrated circuits having one or more digital processing units having either of the following: a.1. A 'total processing performance' of 4800 or more; or a.2. original_interpretation: ECCN 3A090.a currently covers ICs with a TPP of 4800 or more, or a TPP of 1600 or more combined with a performance density of 5.92 or more.

evidence_found: "(6) broadens the country scope for these controls, with respect to the items controlled for RS reasons as well as the advanced computing Foreign Direct Product (FDP) rule and advanced computing provisions in Sec. 744.23, to destinations specified in Country Groups D:1, D:4, and D:5 in supplement no. 1 to part 740 that are not also specified in Country Groups A:5 or A:6" (88 FR 73458, Summary)
original_interpretation: The October 2023 AC/S rule broadened the country scope for advanced computing items to destinations in Country Groups D:1, D:4 and D:5 that are not also in Country Groups A:5 or A:6.

original_interpretation: BIS described the October 2023 AC/S rule as imposing additional licence requirements on exports to more than 40 additional countries to address diversion risk.

evidence_found: "Under new License Exception Notified Advanced Computing (NAC), following receipt of notification for exports and reexports to Macau and destinations identified as subject to a U.S. arms embargo (including China), the U.S. government will determine within 25 days whether the transaction may proceed under the license exception or instead require a license. (BIS page); 88 FR 73458: "new license exception for Notified Advanced Computing (NAC)"
original_interpretation: The October 2023 AC/S rule created License Exception Notified Advanced Computing (NAC), under which, after notification for certain exports (e.g. to Macau and embargoed destinations), the US government determines within 25 days whether the transaction may proceed.

original_interpretation: With the October 2023 rules BIS added two Chinese advanced-chip developers and their subsidiaries (13 entities in total) to the Entity List.

evidence_found: "For our SCAs with price bands, the floor price enables a very robust gross margin for Micron, well above our peak quarterly margins in any past cycle." (Blocks and Files, 25 Jun 2026, quoting CEO Sanjay Mehrotra on FQ3 2026 earnings call)
notes: Correctly typed reported_claim: a company forward-looking statement, not an audited fact.
original_interpretation: Micron said the floor prices in its price-band agreements give a gross margin well above its peak quarterly margins in any past cycle.

correction: The US$100bn is a verbatim CEO statement and is 'over the remaining agreement term'. The US$22bn is a journalist's paraphrase in the article, not a verbatim Micron quote as the evidence field implies. The metric period 'calendar 2026-2030 (approx.)' is not stated by this source (it gives 5-year DC/consumer and 3-year automotive terms); secondary coverage (search result summaries) says 'through calendar 2030' but that was not confirmed from a primary document in this check.
evidence_found: "Fourteen of the 16 SCAs that we have signed have a cumulative revenue at minimum price per our contracts of approximately $100 billion over the remaining agreement term." (CEO quote); "Projections see it receiving cash deposits and related financial commitments of $22 billion." (journalist paraphrase); "They cover the datacenter and consumer markets (5-year duration) and also the automotive sector (3 year duration)." (Blocks and Files, 25 Jun 2026)
notes: Micron's FQ4 2026 results (due late Sept 2026) may update SCA totals; no FQ4 release was found in search as of 2026-09-30.
original_interpretation: Micron said 14 of its 16 Strategic Customer Agreements carry cumulative revenue at contract minimum prices of about US$100 billion, and expected cash deposits and related financial commitments of US$22 billion.

evidence_found: "When completed, we expect approximately half or more of our company revenue to be under these SCAs with customers across end markets." (Blocks and Files, 25 Jun 2026, CEO quote)

evidence_found: "has completed agreements with five major global data center customers and is nearing deals with five other large AI customers."; "Once those are completed, Samsung expects LTAs to cover about 60 to 70 percent of its medium- to long-term memory capacity." (Korea Herald, 12 Aug 2026)
notes: Company statement relayed by news; reported_claim is correct.
original_interpretation: Samsung said it expects long-term agreements to cover about 60-70% of its medium- to long-term memory capacity once pending deals conclude, having finalised agreements with five major data-center customers.

evidence_found: "SK hynix said it has wrapped up LTA negotiations with around 10 customers, including key clients." (Korea Herald, 12 Aug 2026)
notes: The article attributes this to SK hynix itself ('SK hynix said').
original_interpretation: The Korea Herald reported that SK hynix had wrapped up long-term agreement negotiations with around 10 customers by August 2026.

correction: The characterisation is attributed in the article to a July 2026 JPMorgan analysis, not stated by the Korea Herald or the companies. The claim omits the attribution; it also omits 'collateral'. See superseding claim.
evidence_found: JPMorgan's July analysis noted that "newer LTAs increasingly run for three to five years and include pre-agreed supply volumes, pricing formulas or floors and stronger commitments such as prepayments, collateral or financial guarantees."; "Some also use 'take-or-pay' provisions, requiring customers to pay for committed volumes even if they ultimately take fewer chips." (Korea Herald, 12 Aug 2026)
notes: Analyst characterisation relayed by news; should carry attribution to JPMorgan.
original_interpretation: New memory long-term agreements in 2026 increasingly run three to five years with pre-agreed volumes, pricing formulas or floors, prepayments or guarantees, and in some cases take-or-pay clauses.

evidence_found: "Traditional memory deals were generally quarterly or annual arrangements, with relatively flexible volumes and prices frequently renegotiated with the market cycle." (Korea Herald, 12 Aug 2026); Micron 10-K FY2025: customers "typically enter[s] into long-term agreements ... with acknowledgment that pricing, quantity, and other terms will be periodically negotiated to reflect market conditions" (Marketing and Customers)
notes: Two independent publishers are consistent.
original_interpretation: Before 2026, memory supply deals were generally quarterly or annual arrangements with flexible volumes and prices frequently renegotiated with the market cycle.

evidence_found: "LTAs are unlikely to eliminate the memory cycle, but they could reduce earnings volatility by locking in demand for longer periods." (Korea Herald, 12 Aug 2026, unnamed industry official)
notes: Official is unnamed.
original_interpretation: An industry official quoted by the Korea Herald said LTAs are unlikely to eliminate the memory cycle but could reduce earnings volatility.

evidence_found: "OEM contract prices — which comprise 80%-to-90% of all DRAM sales — have remained relatively stable" (EE Times, Jack Robertson, 16 Jul 2002)
notes: Historical (2002) journalist statement; methodology not disclosed. Correctly labelled historical.
original_interpretation: In 2002 EE Times reported that OEM contract prices covered 80-90% of all DRAM sales, leaving the spot market a small and volatile share (historical).

evidence_found: "By contrast, OEM prices are not very open and difficult for most outsiders to track."; "But spot prices are easily tracked from the many exchanges and brokers issuing daily, and sometimes hourly, reports." (EE Times, 16 Jul 2002)
original_interpretation: EE Times noted that OEM contract prices are not openly published and are hard for outsiders to track, while spot prices are widely reported.

evidence_found: DRAMeXchange gathers prices through "direct or indirect survey with associated companies, including manufacturers, distributors, agencies, OEMs, memory card markers…etc."; "Session Average" is the average of all prices within the session, with "Session High" and "Session Low" the highest and lowest (DRAMeXchange FAQ)
notes: Classification: this is DRAMeXchange describing its own methodology on its own site (self-description), so claim_type would more honestly be reported_claim, and the FAQ page is closer to company_documentation than a research_firm report. The content is accurately reproduced.
original_interpretation: DRAMeXchange compiles its price estimates through direct or indirect surveys of manufacturers, distributors, agencies and OEMs, reporting session high, low and average prices.

evidence_found: Contract prices published monthly for DRAM and NAND Flash ("in principle"), with "Mobile DRAM and eMMC/UFS contract price quarterly"; spot prices refreshed three times daily (Opening, Middle, Closing Sessions) (DRAMeXchange FAQ)
notes: Caveat: mobile DRAM and eMMC/UFS contract prices are quarterly, not monthly. Self-description (see CLM-1165 note).
original_interpretation: DRAMeXchange publishes DRAM and NAND contract prices in principle once a month and updates spot prices three times a day.

evidence_found: paraphrase of FAQ: when supply is insufficient the spot price is normally higher than the contract price; the spot price is lower when sellers aggressively move overstocks (DRAMeXchange FAQ, spot vs contract section)
notes: Fetch tool paraphrased; substance matches the researcher's verbatim quote.
original_interpretation: DRAMeXchange describes spot prices as an indication of spot-market supply and demand: above contract prices when supply is short and below them when sellers dump excess inventory.

evidence_found: The spot market comprises "DRAM vendors, OEMs and system integrators (SI), channel distributors, module makers and brokers." (DRAMeXchange FAQ)
notes: Same FAQ also says roughly 5%-10% of monthly production enters the spot market (not part of this claim).
original_interpretation: Spot-market DRAM participants include DRAM vendors, OEMs and system integrators, channel distributors, module makers and brokers.

evidence_found: "Looking only at semiconductors, DRAM rose 7.6% from the previous month and flash memory climbed 19.5%. Compared with a year earlier, those figures surged 259.7% and 223.0%, respectively."; "According to the 'May 2026 Export and Import Price Indexes and Trade Indexes' released by the Bank of Korea on the 16th" (fnnews, 16 Jun 2026)
notes: The paragraph sits in the won-denominated index discussion, suggesting (not stating) a won basis; the claim's methodology note is appropriately cautious. Source is a news report of a BOK release (tier 3); the BOK release itself would be the primary source. Later months (Jun-Aug 2026) exist but do not supersede a May-specific claim.
original_interpretation: The Bank of Korea's export price index showed DRAM prices up 259.7% and flash memory up 223.0% year on year in May 2026.

evidence_found: "In January 2009, Qimonda AG was obliged to file for insolvency"; at its height it employed 13,500 people globally; "Qimonda AG emerged from Infineon Technologies AG in 2006 after Infineon Technologies had transferred its memory chip division to Qimonda" (JAFFE insolvency administrator press release, 26 Aug 2024)
notes: Classification: SRC-0373 is a press release from the insolvency administrator's law firm, a party to the dispute, not a court record. source_type 'court_record' (tier 1) overstates it; 'other' or company_documentation would be more honest. Facts themselves are uncontroversial.
original_interpretation: Qimonda AG, the DRAM maker spun off from Infineon, filed for insolvency in January 2009; at its height it employed 13,500 people.

evidence_found: Settlement amount "800 million euros"; dispute over whether the memory chip division Infineon contributed to Qimonda in 2006 by contribution in kind was of sufficient value; "The creditors' committee of Qimonda AG and the Management Board and Supervisory Board of Infineon Technologies AG have already approved the settlement" (JAFFE release, 26 Aug 2024)
notes: Caveat: the release says Infineon's actual cash payment is EUR 753.5m after offsetting subordinated claims and earlier settlements. Source is a party's press release (see CLM-1170 note on source_type).
original_interpretation: In 2024 Infineon agreed an EUR 800 million settlement with Qimonda's insolvency administrator over the value of the memory business it contributed in the 2006 carve-out.

correction: The licensing and sale to Infineon are supported. The source does not call the portfolio Qimonda's 'main remaining asset'; that characterisation is the researcher's. Also, the patents were mostly licensed before the insolvency, not licensed by the administrator as a step before the sale.
evidence_found: "At the time, Qimonda AG's patent portfolio comprised thousands of patents and patent applications worldwide."; "most of which had been licensed to major market players prior to the insolvency"; "The patent portfolio was finally offered on the market in an international sales process and sold to Infineon Technologies AG as the highest bidder." (JAFFE release, 26 Aug 2024)
original_interpretation: Qimonda's main remaining asset was its patent portfolio, which was licensed and eventually sold to Infineon.

evidence_found: "Hynix Semiconductor Inc. (formerly, Hyundai Electronics Industries Co., Ltd.) ... 44.29 percent"; "All Others 44.29 percent"; "The finding that Samsung Electronics Co., Ltd. ('SEC') received de minimis subsidies did not change."; "except for SEC, which is excluded from this countervailing duty order"; "EFFECTIVE DATE: August 11, 2003." (68 FR 47546-47547)
notes: Rate is a cash-deposit net subsidy rate; duties applied to entries on or after 7 Apr 2003 (preliminary determination).
original_interpretation: In August 2003 the US imposed a countervailing duty of 44.29% on DRAMs from Hynix (formerly Hyundai Electronics), while Samsung was found to have received de minimis subsidies and was excluded.

correction: The year 2009 is not stated in SRC-0375. It is supported by IndustryWeek (30 Jun 2009): Elpida "will sell securities worth 30 billion yen to the government-backed Development Bank of Japan" (new claim added). The 80% loss coverage is a feature of the scheme generally, as described by Nippon.com.
evidence_found: "a mechanism was introduced for the Development Bank of Japan to invest in businesses that had insufficient capital, conditional upon joint investment by private enterprise, and for the government to cover 80% of any losses that occured."; "Elpida was the first business to benefit from this investment scheme when it received ¥30 billion from the DBJ." (Nippon.com column, 2 May 2012)
notes: SRC-0375 publication_date is 2012-05-02 per the page, not 'unknown'.
original_interpretation: In 2009 the Development Bank of Japan invested JPY 30 billion in Elpida under the revised Industrial Revitalization Act, with the government covering 80% of any losses.

evidence_found: "the company went to the courts to seek shelter against liabilities totaling ￥448 billion (US$5.53 billion)"; "the punishingly high yen, global market volatility and fierce competition with South Korean and Taiwanese rivals have made life difficult"; Akita Elpida separately filed with ¥7.9 billion of liabilities (Taipei Times/AFP, 28 Feb 2012)
notes: Filing date 27 Feb 2012 ('yesterday'); ¥448bn excludes Akita Elpida as the metric states.
original_interpretation: Elpida filed for bankruptcy protection in February 2012 with liabilities of JPY 448 billion (about US$5.5 billion), amid a strong yen and competition from Korean and Taiwanese rivals.

evidence_found: "By the end of this year, only three DRAM manufacturers will remain—Samsung and SK Hynix of South Korea, and U.S.-based Micron Technology."; "Notable DRAM makers Qimonda of Germany and Elpida Memory of Japan have gone bankrupt and have been bought out by other players." (eeNews Europe, 19 Jun 2013, citing Mike Howard, IHS)
notes: A 2013 forecast; correctly typed estimate. Ignores Chinese/Taiwanese niche DRAM makers (e.g., Nanya, Winbond), which IHS evidently discounted; later entrants (CXMT) post-date it.
original_interpretation: IHS said in 2013 that by year-end only three DRAM manufacturers would remain (Samsung, SK hynix and Micron), after Qimonda and Elpida went bankrupt and were bought out.

evidence_found: "Global semiconductor industry sales were $412.1 billion in 2019, a decrease of 12.1 percent compared to the 2018 total."; memory down 32.6%, DRAM down 37.1%, NAND flash down 25.9% (SIA release, 3 Feb 2020)
original_interpretation: SIA reported that memory sales fell 32.6% in 2019, with DRAM down 37.1% and NAND flash down 25.9%, while total semiconductor sales fell 12.1% to US$412.1 billion.

evidence_found: John Neuffer, SIA president and CEO, cited "ongoing global trade unrest and cyclicality in product pricing" (SIA release, 3 Feb 2020)
original_interpretation: SIA attributed the 2019 downturn to global trade unrest and cyclicality in product pricing.

evidence_found: "Worldwide semiconductor sales fell an expected 32% in 2001 with the industry posting the sharpest yearly decline in its history"; sales of $139 billion in 2001, down from $204 billion in 2000 (EE Times, 4 Feb 2002, reporting SIA)
notes: 'In its history' as of 2002; later declines (e.g., 2009, 2023) were smaller in percentage terms.
original_interpretation: World semiconductor sales fell 32% in 2001 to US$139 billion from US$204 billion, the sharpest yearly decline in the industry's history at the time.

evidence_found: "when the popular 16-megabit DRAM chip dropped from $70 wholesale a year ago to $7 this summer, profits disappeared completely" (Christian Science Monitor, 4 Oct 1996)
notes: 'A year ago' relative to Oct 1996 gives roughly mid/late 1995; journalist figure, no methodology.
original_interpretation: The 16-megabit DRAM wholesale price fell from about US$70 in mid-1995 to about US$7 by summer 1996.

evidence_found: "Chipmakers built so many new manufacturing plants, called fabs, during the first half of the 1990s that they have too much capacity for a computer market that has slackened from its roaring pace a year ago." (CSM, 4 Oct 1996)
original_interpretation: The Christian Science Monitor attributed the 1996 DRAM collapse to chipmakers building too many fabs in the first half of the 1990s as PC demand slowed.

evidence_found: "The rules include new controls on 24 types of semiconductor manufacturing equipment and 3 types of software tools for developing or producing semiconductors; new controls on high-bandwidth memory (HBM); new red flag guidance to address compliance and diversion concerns; 140 Entity List additions and 14 modifications spanning PRC tool manufacturers, semiconductor fabs, and investment companies" (BIS press release, 2 Dec 2024, p.1). original_interpretation: The December 2024 BIS package added controls on 24 types of semiconductor manufacturing equipment and 3 types of software tools, new controls on high-bandwidth memory, red-flag guidance, and 140 Entity List additions plus 14 modifications.

evidence_found: "New controls on semiconductor manufacturing equipment needed to produce advanced-node integrated circuits, including certain etch, deposition, lithography, ion implantation, annealing, metrology and inspection, and cleaning tools." (BIS press release, 2 Dec 2024, p.3)

evidence_found: "The new controls apply to U.S.-origin HBM as well as foreign-produced HBM subject to the EAR under the advanced computing Foreign Direct Product (FDP) rule. Certain HBM will be eligible for authorization under new License Exception HBM." (BIS press release, 2 Dec 2024, p.3)

evidence_found: "Under new 3A090.c, this IFR will control HBM having a `memory bandwidth density' greater than 2 GB per second per square millimeter (mm). All HBM stacks currently in production exceed this threshold." (89 FR 96790, preamble, FR p. 96800)

original_interpretation: New ECCN 3A090.c (December 2024) controls HBM with a memory bandwidth density greater than 2 GB per second per square millimetre.

evidence_found: "Semiconductor Manufacturing Equipment (SME) FDP: Extends jurisdiction over specified foreign-produced SME and related items if there is 'knowledge' that the foreign-produced commodity is destined to Macau or a destination in Country Group D:5, including the PRC." (BIS press release, 2 Dec 2024, p.3)
original_interpretation: The December 2024 SME FDP rule extends US jurisdiction over specified foreign-produced semiconductor manufacturing equipment and related items when there is knowledge they are destined to Macau or a Country Group D:5 destination, including China.

evidence_found: "Footnote 5 (FN5) FDP: Extends jurisdiction over specified foreign-produced SME and related items if there is 'knowledge' of certain involvement by an entity on or added to the Entity List with a FN5 designation. Such entities are being designated ... such as these entities' involvement in supporting the PRC's military modernization through the PRC's attempts to produce advanced-node semiconductors" (BIS press release, 2 Dec 2024, p.3)
original_interpretation: The December 2024 Footnote 5 (FN5) FDP rule extends US jurisdiction over specified foreign-produced SME when there is knowledge of involvement by an Entity List party designated with footnote 5, such as entities supporting China's advanced-node chip production.

evidence_found: Press release: "De minimis: Extends jurisdiction over specified foreign-produced SME and related items described in the above FDP rules that contain any amount of U.S.-origin integrated circuits." (p.3). FR: "Section 734.4(a)(8) specifies that there is no de minimis threshold level of U.S. controlled content for commodities specified in ECCNs 3B001.a.4, c, d, f.1, f.5, k to n, p.2, p.4, r, or 3B002.c when the commodity is incorporated in a U.S.- origin IC or contains a U.S.-origin IC specified under Category 3, 4, or 5 of the CCL, and the commodity is destined for Macau or a destination specified in Country Group D:5, unless excluded ..." (89 FR 96790, FR p. 96796)
notes: The researcher's FR quote was truncated mid-sentence. The legal text limits the provision to listed ECCNs, U.S.-origin ICs in CCL Categories 3-5, and Macau/D:5 destinations (734.4(a)(8)), with a parallel 734.4(a)(9) for FN5 cases; the claim's simplified wording matches the press release.
original_interpretation: The December 2024 rules added a de minimis provision extending US jurisdiction over specified foreign-produced SME covered by the new FDP rules if it contains any amount of US-origin integrated circuits.

evidence_found: "New software and technology controls, including restrictions on Electronic Computer Aided Design (ECAD) and Technology Computer Aided Design (TCAD) software and technology when there is 'knowledge' that such items will be used for the design of advanced-node integrated circuits to be produced in Macau or a destination in Country Group D:5." (BIS press release, 2 Dec 2024, p.4)

original_interpretation: The December 2024 rules clarified that export controls apply to software keys that give access to hardware or software or renew existing software and hardware use licences.

evidence_found: FR API record: citation "90 FR 5298"; publication_date 2025-01-16; effective_on 2025-01-16; dates: "The effective date of this rule is January 16, 2025."; title "Implementation of Additional Due Diligence Measures for Advanced Computing Integrated Circuits; Amendments and Clarifications; and Extension of Comment Period"; abstract: "This interim final rule (IFR) will protect the national security of the United States and assist foundries and Outsourced Semiconductor Assembly and Test (\"OSATs\") companies in complying with provisions of the EAR"
notes: Full official title continues '; Amendments and Clarifications; and Extension of Comment Period'. The researcher's abstract quote was abridged (not verbatim). It is an interim final rule.
original_interpretation: The foundry/OSAT due-diligence rule is 90 FR 5298, 'Implementation of Additional Due Diligence Measures for Advanced Computing Integrated Circuits', published and effective 16 January 2025.

correction: The 'no HBM' condition applies only to the higher 35bn (2027) and 40bn (2029 or later) thresholds; an IC below 30bn transistors qualifies whether or not it contains HBM. The transistor-count route requires an attestation by the front-end fabricator (if it packages the die outside Macau/D:5) or by an approved OSAT. 'Applicable advanced logic ICs' also include any logic IC using a non-planar transistor architecture, not only 16/14 nm or below. The rule text sets no separate threshold for 2028.
evidence_found: Note 1 to 3A090.a (90 FR 5298, FR p. 5314): "there is a presumption that the item is 3A090.a and designed or marketed for datacenters ... A 'front-end fabricator' or 'OSAT' company can overcome this presumption in any of the following three ways ... b. If the integrated circuit die is packaged by the 'front-end fabricator' at a location outside of Macau or a destination specified in Country Group D:5 ..., then the attestation of the 'front-end fabricator' that (a) the 'aggregated approximated transistor count' of the final packaged IC is below 30 billion transistors, or (b) the final packaged IC does not contain high-bandwidth memory and that the 'aggregated approximated transistor count' of the final packaged IC is below (i) 35 billion transistors for any exports ... completed in 2027; or (ii) 40 billion transistors for any exports ... completed in 2029 or thereafter". Definition (772.1): "Applicable advanced logic integrated circuits are logic integrated circuits produced using the '16/14 nanometer node' or below, or using a non-planar transistor architecture."
notes: Researcher evidence was a tool paraphrase; checker obtained verbatim regulatory text. Corrected claim added.
original_interpretation: Under the January 2025 due-diligence rule, a logic IC produced at the 16/14 nm node or below that a front-end fabricator or OSAT exports is presumed to be ECCN 3A090.a unless the designer is approved or authorised, or the packaged IC has fewer than 30 billion transistors (35 billion from 2027, 40 billion from 2029) and no HBM, or an approved OSAT attests.

evidence_found: 90 FR 5298 preamble (FR p. 5302): "New supplement no. 6 to part 740 ... lists as approved IC designers Advanced Micro Devices, Inc., Alphabet Inc., ... and Western Digital Technologies, Inc." (checker count: 33) and "Supplement no. 7 to part 740 lists the following companies as approved 'OSAT' companies ... Amkor Technology, Inc., ... and United Microelectronics Corporation (UMC)." (checker count: 24). Note 1 to 3A090.a: authorized IC designers are those "(i) Headquartered in Taiwan or a destination specified in Country Group A:1 or A:5, that are neither located in nor have an ultimate parent headquartered in Macau or a destination specified in Country Group D:5 ...; and (ii) That have agreed to submit applicable information described in Sec. 743.9(b) to the 'front-end fabricator'".
notes: Checker independently counted 33 designers and 24 OSATs. eCFR Supplement No. 6 to Part 740 as of 2026-09-01 still lists the same 33 designers (unchanged since 90 FR 5310).
original_interpretation: The January 2025 rule published lists of approved IC designers (supplement no. 6, 33 companies per the rule) and approved OSATs (supplement no. 7, 24 companies), and defined 'authorized IC designers' as designers headquartered in Taiwan or Country Group A:1 or A:5 destinations meeting criteria and reporting requirements.

correction: The KYC form and quarterly reporting obligation in Sec. 743.9 fall on front-end fabricators only, not on OSATs. Reports cover 3A090.a (or presumed 3A090.a) ICs produced for authorized designers; the first report was due 31 May 2025.
evidence_found: 15 CFR 743.9(a) as added by 90 FR 5298 (FR p. 5310): "'Front-end fabricators' producing any integrated circuit specified under ECCN 3A090.a or presumed to be specified under ECCN 3A090.a by Note 1 to 3A090 for any authorized integrated circuit designer must submit reports to BIS"; 743.9(b)(3): "The end-user Know Your Customer (KYC) vetting form included in supplement no. 2 of this part"; 743.9(c): "Quarterly reporting requirement. (1) You must submit the first report by May 31, 2025."
notes: Researcher evidence was a tool paraphrase, not verbatim. Corrected claim added.
original_interpretation: Under the January 2025 rule, front-end fabricators and OSATs must run know-your-customer checks on authorised (non-approved) IC designers using a BIS form and submit quarterly reports to BIS on those transactions.

evidence_found: FR API record 2026-06851: citation "91 FR 17851"; publication_date 2026-04-09; effective_on 2026-04-07; abstract: "extending by about eight months the triggering date for authorized integrated circuit designer status and submission date for applications to become an approved integrated circuit (IC) designer. Federal Register API search found no later rule on IC designers published after 2026-04-10 (as of 2026-09-30). The researcher's 'a delay of approximately eight months' wording is not in the current abstract ('by about eight months'); substance unchanged.
original_interpretation: A BIS rule effective 7 April 2026 (91 FR 17851) extended authorised IC designer status and the deadline to apply to become an approved IC designer to 31 December 2026, a delay of about eight months.

evidence_found: "ECAD software controlled under new ECCN 3D006 requires a license for NS and AT reasons, respectively, for countries with an 'X' listed in columns NS:2 or AT:1 on the Commerce Country Chart." NS Column 2 ... AT Column 1".

correction: Accurate for the October 2022 text only. As amended through January 2025, 744.6(c)(2) now covers Macau and all Country Group D:5 destinations (not only the PRC), keys on facilities of Macau/D:5-headquartered entities producing 'advanced-node ICs', and the end-use-free SME prong references 3B001/3B002/3D992/3E992 items, not ECCN 3B090 (no longer referenced).
evidence_found: 87 FR 62186 (FR p. 62193-94): "new paragraph (c)(2) informs 'U.S. persons' that the shipment, transmission, or transfer (in-country) to or within the PRC of any item not subject to the EAR; facilitation of such shipment, transmission, or transfer (in-country); or servicing of any item not subject to the EAR to or within the PRC when such activity would assist the 'development' or 'production' of ICs meeting certain parameters is subject to a license requirement"; "...meeting the parameters of ECCN 3B090, 3D001 (for 3B090), or 3E001 (for 3B090) regardless of end use or end user". Current 15 CFR 744.6(c)(2) (eCFR as of 2026-09-01): covers items not subject to the EAR "To or within Macau or a destination specified in Country Group D:5" for development/production of ICs at a 'facility' of a Macau/D:5-headquartered entity where advanced-node ICs are produced; and "(iii) Semiconductor manufacturing equipment. To or within either Macau or a destination specified in Country Group D:5, any item not subject to the EAR and meeting the parameters of ECCNs 3B001.a.4, c, d, f.1, f.5, f.6, k to n, p.2, p.4, r, 3B002.c, 3D992, or 3E992 regardless of end use or end user." Amendment history: 88 FR 73448, 73494 (Oct 2023); 89 FR 23885; 89 FR 96817; 90 FR 5311.
notes: Corrected claim added citing eCFR 15 CFR 744.6 as of 2026-09-01 (new source in this batch).
original_interpretation: Since October 2022, 15 CFR 744.6(c)(2) requires US persons to have a licence to ship, transmit or transfer to or within China, facilitate such transfers, or service items not subject to the EAR when this supports development or production of ICs at specified advanced Chinese fabs, and for items meeting ECCN 3B090 parameters regardless of end use.

correction: The October 2022 policy (denial except US/A:5/A:6-headquartered end users in China) has been replaced. Current policy: presumption of denial for Macau/D:5 destinations and Macau/D:5-headquartered entities; case-by-case for listed exceptions and all other applications; review factors now include contract sanctity.
evidence_found: 87 FR 62186 (FR p. 62194): "there is a presumption of denial for applications to export, reexport, or transfer (in-country) items subject to the license requirements of Sec. 744.6(c)(2) except for license applications for end users in China headquartered in the United States or in a country in Country Group A:5 or A:6, which will be considered on a case-by-case basis taking into account factors including technology level, customers and compliance plans." Current 744.6(e)(3) (eCFR 2026-09-01): "License review will take into account factors including technology level, customers, compliance plans, and contract sanctity. (i) Presumption of denial. Applications will be reviewed with a presumption of denial for Macau and destinations specified in Country Group D:5 and entities headquartered or whose ultimate parent is headquartered in Macau or destinations specified in Country Group D:5, unless paragraph (e)(3)(ii) of this section applies. (ii) Case-by-case ... (C) For all other applications not specified in paragraph (e)(3)(i) ..."
notes: Corrected claim added citing eCFR 15 CFR 744.6 as of 2026-09-01.
original_interpretation: Licence applications under the US-persons restriction face a presumption of denial, except those for end users in China headquartered in the US or in Country Group A:5 or A:6 countries, which are reviewed case by case considering technology level, customers and compliance plans.

correction: The definition includes packaging and testing, so logic packaging and test done by OSATs is inside Foundry 2.0, and adding OSAT totals to Foundry 2.0 would double count. TSMC does not publish Foundry 2.0 components, so the size of the overlap is unknown.
evidence_found: "the foundry 2.0 industry, which we define as all logic wafer manufacturing, packaging, testing, mask-making and others" (TSMC 4Q25 call, p. 5).

correction: The ratios are arithmetically right, but every input is a forecast (2007, 2017), not an actual. The second half ('no public estimate shows a large change since then') is contradicted by the same research unit's CLM-1117, which shows about 43% for the mid-2020s from DIGITIMES and SIA/BCG. Restate as: outsourced share was about 44% (2007 forecast) and about 53% (2017 forecast, 2019 CSET); post-2019 public data give inconsistent pictures (about 43% if DIGITIMES 2024 OSAT revenue is set against SIA/BCG's US$95bn) because definitions differ.
evidence_found: Recomputed from re-opened sources: 21.1/48.16 = 43.8% (Gartner Dataquest 2007 forecast, SST); 28.1/53.3 = 52.7% (Gartner 2017 forecast, Semiconductor Engineering); CSET 2019 28/53 = 52.8% (CLM-1037, verified). The researcher's own CLM-1117 computes 41.2/95 = 43% for 2024 (DIGITIMES OSAT revenue vs SIA/BCG ATP market).
notes: See the contradictions record with CLM-1117.
original_interpretation: Across published Gartner-based estimates, the outsourced share of assembly, packaging and test value rose from about 44% (2007 forecast) to about 52-53% by 2016-2019, and no public estimate shows a large change since then.

evidence_found: Recomputed: 41.2 / 95 = 43.4%; 28.1 / 53.3 = 52.7%. SIA/BCG (May 2024, PDF p. 20): "The $95 billion ATP market is currently concentrated in Northeast Asia." No reference year is given for the US$95bn. DIGITIMES US$41.2bn (2024) is in verified CLM-1026.

original_interpretation: Setting DIGITIMES' 2024 OSAT revenue (US$41.2bn) against SIA/BCG's US$95bn ATP market implies OSATs perform only about 43% of back-end value, lower than the ~53% implied by Gartner 2017 and CSET 2019; the gap is likely definitional (SIA/BCG's total may value in-house and foundry advanced packaging generously) rather than evidence of insourcing.
